Neonatal Silky sharks (Carcharhinus falciformis) emerge from their mothers at a modest size, with field records indicating a total length at birth of approximately 69 cm [Lb = approximately 69 cm]. This relatively small birth size is typical of viviparous carcharhinids and places the newborn pups in a size range that makes them vulnerable to predation by larger pelagic fishes, including conspecifics. The aplacental viviparous embryos develop within the uterus, sustained initially by a yolk sac before transitioning to a form of histotrophic nutrition. Following parturition, the pups are entirely independent, exhibiting a rapid growth phase during their early juvenile years. Data from the eastern Pacific suggest that these young individuals face high natural mortality rates, which imposes strong selective pressure on achieving a larger body size quickly to reduce predation risk.

For Silky sharks inhabiting tropical waters, reproductive activity has been documented under thermal conditions that are consistently warm. In the Gulf of Mexico and throughout the Indo-Pacific, studies conducted at a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] have recorded a maximum reproductive rate that translates to 8 to 10 pups per litter [N_R_i = 8 to 10 pups per litter], with females producing a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year]. This modest annual fecundity, consisting of a single litter of moderately sized pups, is characteristic of slow-growing elasmobranchs with an extended gestation period. The litter size itself can range from 8 to 10 pups, a relatively narrow range that reflects the constraints imposed by the uterine space and the energetic demands of intrauterine development. The underlying physiological mechanism driving this reproductive output involves ovulation followed by internal fertilisation, after which the gestating embryos undergo a lengthy developmental period.

Female Silky sharks attain sexual maturity after a substantial period of growth, with puberty occurring at a total length of 215 cm [Lp = 215 cm]. This somatic milestone is reached after an extended juvenile phase, reflecting the species' relatively slow life-history pace. In comparative terms, this length at maturation is intermediate among large-bodied carcharhinids; for instance, it is smaller than the reported size at maturity for the tiger shark yet larger than that observed in the blacktip shark. Data from the western Atlantic and Indian Oceans indicate that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 9.5 years [tp = approximately 9.5 years] when considered within the context of warm thermal regimes at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This delayed maturation is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises somatic growth and the accumulation of lipid reserves before the onset of gonadal maturation.

Adult female Silky sharks exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 332 cm [Li = 332 cm], making them one of the larger pelagic carcharhinids. This ultimate length for females is rarely attained, as most individuals experience natural mortality before reaching such an advanced age. The maximum lifespan for this species has been estimated at 34 years [am = 34 years] under the stable thermal conditions found in tropical seas at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This considerable longevity aligns with the species' low reproductive output and late maturity, both of which are hallmarks of a K-selected life-history strategy. Comparisons with related species such as the dusky shark reveal similar longevity estimates and confirm that large carcharhinids are among the longest-lived members of the elasmobranch lineage.

The deep-bodied physique of the Silky shark, combined with its large pectoral fins and streamlined body, is an adaptation for efficient cruising in open-ocean habitats. Juveniles are frequently observed in association with floating objects, including drifting seaweed and fish aggregation devices, which offer shelter and concentrated prey. The species displays a pronounced ontogenetic shift in diet, with younger individuals feeding predominantly on squid and small pelagic fishes, while adults consume larger prey. Field observations of stomach contents have revealed that Silky sharks are opportunistic predators with a broad trophic niche. Under warm tropical sea conditions at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum lifespan reaches 34 years [am = 34 years], underscoring the species' vulnerability to overfishing due to its slow life history.
